title: Katz, quanta, and vesicles
text:
CHAPTER 6. CHEMICAL TRANSMISSION
SECTION 6.2. KATZ, QUANTA, AND VESICLES

The neuromuscular junction as a model synapse

Once it was accepted that the neuromuscular junction uses acetylcholine, the next question was how the release works. How much transmitter is released by one nerve impulse? Is it released continuously, like water from a tap, or in discrete packets? What triggers it? The person who answered these questions most clearly was Bernard Katz (1911 to 2003).

Katz was born in Leipzig, Germany. Being Jewish, he left Nazi Germany in 1935 and moved to London, where he worked with A. V. Hill at University College London. He spent part of the war years in Australia, working with John Eccles and Stephen Kuffler in Sydney, and served in the Royal Australian Air Force as a radar officer. After the war he returned to University College London, where he spent the rest of his career. He collaborated with Hodgkin and Huxley on the ionic basis of the action potential (section 5.1), and then turned to the synapse.

The neuromuscular junction of the frog was an ideal preparation. It is large, accessible, and isolated: each muscle fiber is usually contacted by one motor nerve terminal. With glass microelectrodes, which had been developed for intracellular recording in the late 1940s (Gilbert Ling and Ralph Gerard are credited with an important version of the technique), Katz and his colleagues could record the voltage inside a muscle fiber right at the junction. The postsynaptic response at the neuromuscular junction is called the end-plate potential (EPP), because the region of muscle membrane under the nerve terminal is called the end plate. Normally, the EPP is large enough to trigger a muscle action potential, ensuring that every nerve impulse produces a muscle twitch. To study the EPP itself, Katz used curare (which partly blocks acetylcholine receptors) or low calcium solutions to reduce it below threshold.

Miniature end-plate potentials

In 1950 to 1952, Paul Fatt and Bernard Katz noticed something unexpected. When they recorded from the end plate without stimulating the nerve, they saw small, spontaneous depolarizations, each about 0.5 to 1 millivolt in amplitude, occurring at random intervals, roughly one per second on average. They called these miniature end-plate potentials (MEPPs, or "minis").

Several observations showed that MEPPs were caused by spontaneous release of acetylcholine from the nerve terminal:

- They occurred only at the end plate, not elsewhere along the muscle fiber.
- They were blocked by curare, which blocks acetylcholine receptors.
- They were increased in size and duration by neostigmine, which blocks acetylcholinesterase.
- They disappeared when the nerve was cut and the terminal degenerated.

The most striking feature was that MEPPs all had roughly the same size. This suggested that acetylcholine was released in fixed packets, each producing a MEPP. Fatt and Katz published these findings in 1952.

The quantal hypothesis

Jose del Castillo and Bernard Katz then took the next step. In 1954 they studied EPPs evoked by nerve stimulation under conditions of reduced release (low calcium, high magnesium). Under these conditions, the EPP evoked by each nerve impulse fluctuated in size from trial to trial. Sometimes there was no response at all (a "failure"). Sometimes there was a response about the size of one MEPP. Sometimes two MEPPs, sometimes three, and so on. When they plotted a histogram of EPP amplitudes, it had peaks at integer multiples of the MEPP amplitude.

Del Castillo and Katz proposed the quantal hypothesis: transmitter is released in discrete packets, called quanta, each containing a fixed amount of transmitter. A nerve impulse releases a variable number of quanta. Under normal conditions, a nerve impulse at the frog neuromuscular junction releases on the order of a hundred or more quanta, producing a large EPP. Under low calcium, it releases only a few, and the quantal nature becomes visible.

The statistics of release

Del Castillo and Katz modeled release statistically. Suppose the nerve terminal has n release sites, each of which releases one quantum with probability p in response to an impulse, independently. Then the number of quanta released, k, follows a binomial distribution:

  P(k) = C(n, k) * p^k * (1 - p)^(n - k)

where C(n, k) is the binomial coefficient. The mean number of quanta released is m = n * p, called the quantal content.

When p is small and n is large (as under low calcium), the binomial distribution is well approximated by the Poisson distribution:

  P(k) = exp(-m) * m^k / k!

Del Castillo and Katz tested this model in several ways. One elegant test uses failures. Under the Poisson model, the probability of zero quanta (a failure) is P(0) = exp(-m). So m can be estimated as

  m = ln( number of trials / number of failures )

Another estimate of m is the ratio of the mean EPP amplitude to the mean MEPP amplitude. The two estimates agreed well, supporting the model. The full distribution of EPP amplitudes, with each peak broadened by the natural variability of quantal size, also matched the Poisson predictions.

This is one of the earliest and most elegant applications of probability theory in neuroscience. It turned a fluctuating, noisy signal into evidence about a hidden mechanism. In modern terms, it is a latent variable model: the observed amplitude is generated by a hidden count (number of quanta) multiplied by a quantal size plus noise, and the parameters can be inferred from the distribution of observations. The same "quantal analysis" approach was later applied to central synapses, though there it is harder because the quanta are smaller and the noise is larger.

Calcium triggers release

Katz and Ricardo Miledi showed in the 1960s that calcium ions are essential for release. Release depends steeply on the external calcium concentration. In some classic experiments, they applied calcium briefly from a pipette at different times relative to the arrival of the nerve impulse, and found that calcium must be present at the moment the impulse arrives in the terminal, not before or after. They proposed the calcium hypothesis: depolarization of the nerve terminal opens voltage-gated calcium channels, calcium flows in, and the rise in calcium inside the terminal triggers release.

The relationship between calcium and release is highly nonlinear. Measurements by Francis Dodge and Rami Rahamimoff in 1967 suggested that release is proportional roughly to the fourth power of the calcium concentration (under their conditions), implying that several calcium ions must bind to a sensor cooperatively to trigger release of a vesicle. This steep dependence means that small changes in calcium entry produce large changes in release, which makes release very sensitive to modulation.

Vesicles

What are the quanta physically? Around the same time that Katz developed the quantal hypothesis, electron microscopists were obtaining the first clear images of synapses (section 4.1). They saw that presynaptic terminals are filled with small, round, membrane-bound sacs, about 40 to 50 nanometers in diameter, called synaptic vesicles. It was natural to propose that each vesicle contains one quantum of transmitter, and that release occurs when a vesicle fuses with the presynaptic membrane and empties its contents into the synaptic cleft (exocytosis). Biochemical studies later showed that vesicles do contain acetylcholine (or other transmitters), and estimates suggested a few thousand acetylcholine molecules per vesicle at the neuromuscular junction.

Direct evidence for vesicle fusion came in the 1970s from John Heuser, Thomas Reese, and colleagues. They used a technique of rapid freezing: a stimulated frog neuromuscular junction was slammed against a block of copper cooled by liquid helium, freezing it within milliseconds of stimulation. Freeze-fracture electron microscopy then revealed vesicles fused with the membrane at specialized release sites (active zones) just after stimulation, and the number of fusions correlated with the number of quanta released, as estimated electrophysiologically. They also traced how vesicle membrane is retrieved and recycled after fusion (endocytosis).

Katz received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1970, shared with Ulf von Euler and Julius Axelrod, "for their discoveries concerning the humoral transmitters in the nerve terminals and the mechanism for their storage, release and inactivation."

The molecular machinery

In the following decades, the proteins that carry out vesicle fusion were identified. The central players are the SNARE proteins, which include synaptobrevin (also called VAMP) on the vesicle and syntaxin and SNAP-25 on the presynaptic membrane. These proteins wind together into a tight bundle, pulling the vesicle and plasma membranes together and driving their fusion. Synaptotagmin, a protein on the vesicle, binds calcium and acts as a calcium sensor that triggers fast, synchronous release. Other proteins, such as Munc18 and Munc13 and complexin, regulate the process.

James Rothman, Randy Schekman, and Thomas Sudhof shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries of the machinery regulating vesicle traffic. Rothman and Schekman worked out much of the general machinery of vesicle trafficking in cells, and Sudhof worked out how synaptotagmin and other proteins make release at synapses calcium-dependent and fast.

Interestingly, some of the most potent toxins known act on this machinery. Botulinum toxins and tetanus toxin are enzymes that cut specific SNARE proteins, blocking transmitter release. Botulinum toxin blocks release at the neuromuscular junction, causing paralysis; in tiny, controlled doses, it is used in medicine to treat muscle spasms and in cosmetics to reduce wrinkles. Tetanus toxin acts mainly on inhibitory synapses in the spinal cord, causing uncontrolled muscle contraction. The toxins were valuable tools for identifying the roles of the SNARE proteins.

Synapses are unreliable, and that may be useful

At the neuromuscular junction, release is reliable because there are many release sites. A nerve impulse almost always produces a muscle action potential; the "safety factor" is high. But at many synapses in the central nervous system, things are different. A typical synapse between two cortical neurons may have one or a few release sites, and the probability that a vesicle is released in response to a given action potential can be low, sometimes around 0.1 to 0.5, and varies widely between synapses. So many action potentials arriving at such a synapse produce no release at all.

This seems wasteful. Why would the brain use unreliable connections? Several hypotheses have been proposed:

- Energy efficiency. Releasing transmitter and restoring gradients after postsynaptic currents costs energy. Unreliable synapses save energy, and since many synapses converge on each neuron, the overall signal may still be transmitted adequately.
- Dynamic filtering. Release probability changes with recent activity, which allows synapses to act as filters (see short-term plasticity, below).
- Computation with noise. Randomness may help the brain to explore, to sample from probability distributions, or to avoid getting stuck.
- Regularization. Random failures may prevent the network from relying too much on any single connection, similar to dropout in artificial networks.

Short-term plasticity

The strength of a synapse also changes on short time scales, from milliseconds to minutes, depending on its recent activity. This is called short-term synaptic plasticity. Two main forms are:

- Facilitation: when two action potentials arrive in quick succession, the second may release more transmitter than the first. This is thought to be due mainly to residual calcium in the terminal from the first impulse adding to the calcium entry from the second.
- Depression: with repeated stimulation, release decreases, often because the pool of vesicles ready to be released is depleted faster than it can be refilled.

Synapses with high initial release probability tend to depress; synapses with low release probability tend to facilitate. A widely used mathematical model of short-term plasticity was proposed by Misha Tsodyks and Henry Markram in 1997. In a simplified version, each synapse has a variable x, representing the fraction of available resources (vesicles), and a variable u, representing the utilization (release probability). At each spike, a fraction u of the available resources is used, so the postsynaptic response is proportional to u * x. Between spikes, x recovers toward 1 with a time constant tau_rec, and u relaxes toward a baseline U with a time constant tau_facil. In plain text:

  between spikes:  dx/dt = (1 - x) / tau_rec
                   du/dt = (U - u) / tau_facil
  at each spike:   u -> u + U * (1 - u)       (facilitation)
                   response proportional to u * x
                   x -> x - u * x              (depletion)

(Different papers order these updates slightly differently.) With small U and long tau_facil, the synapse facilitates; with large U and long tau_rec, it depresses.

Depressing synapses act like high-pass filters or gain controls: they respond strongly to changes in input rate but weakly to sustained high rates. One consequence, pointed out by Larry Abbott, Kamal Sen, Juan Varela, and Sacha Nelson in 1997, is that depressing synapses can implement a form of gain control, making a neuron sensitive to relative rather than absolute changes in its inputs' firing rates. Facilitating synapses act more like low-pass filters or burst detectors, responding most strongly to sustained high-frequency trains.

Bridge to AI: noisy weights, dropout, and dynamic synapses

Quantal release offers several useful connections to AI.

Stochastic weights. In a standard artificial network, a weight is a fixed real number, and transmission through a connection is deterministic. In the brain, a synapse is a noisy channel with a release probability, a quantal size, and a number of release sites. The effective "weight" is the expected response, but each transmission is random. Some machine learning methods use this idea. Dropout randomly drops units or connections during training. "DropConnect," proposed around 2013, randomly drops individual weights, which is closer to synaptic failure. Bayesian neural networks treat weights as probability distributions rather than fixed values, which allows the network to represent uncertainty about its parameters. Some theorists have suggested that synaptic variability in the brain could serve a similar purpose, representing uncertainty about the right strength of each synapse, a hypothesis sometimes discussed under the name "synaptic sampling."

Low-precision computation. The brain transmits information through a small number of discrete vesicles, effectively a low-precision, quantized signal. AI hardware increasingly uses low-precision arithmetic (8-bit, 4-bit, or even binary weights and activations) to save energy and memory, and quantized networks can perform surprisingly well. The brain is evidence that powerful computation is possible with noisy, low-precision components.

Dynamic synapses as temporal filters. Short-term plasticity makes each synapse a small dynamical system that filters its input. Artificial networks usually place all the dynamics in the units (for example, in recurrent connections), not in the weights. But there is growing interest in "fast weights," an idea discussed by Geoffrey Hinton and others since the 1980s, in which weights change rapidly during processing to store recent information. Fast weights are related to short-term plasticity. In 2016, Jimmy Ba, Geoffrey Hinton, and colleagues proposed using fast weights to attend to the recent past, and later researchers, including Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie, and Jurgen Schmidhuber in 2021, pointed out a formal connection between linear transformers (a variant of the transformer architecture) and fast weight programmers. In this view, the attention mechanism of a transformer can be seen as a kind of rapidly updated synaptic memory.

Summary

- Fatt and Katz (1952) discovered miniature end-plate potentials, spontaneous responses of nearly constant size.
- Del Castillo and Katz (1954) proposed that transmitter is released in quanta; evoked responses fluctuate as integer multiples of the quantal size, following binomial or Poisson statistics.
- Katz and Miledi showed that calcium entry triggers release; release depends steeply (about the fourth power) on calcium.
- Quanta correspond to synaptic vesicles, whose fusion was captured by rapid freezing; Katz shared the 1970 Nobel Prize.
- SNARE proteins and synaptotagmin drive and trigger fusion (Nobel 2013); botulinum and tetanus toxins cut SNAREs.
- Central synapses are often unreliable, and short-term facilitation and depression make synapses dynamic filters; these ideas connect to dropout, Bayesian weights, quantization, and fast weights in AI.
